summary: Ukraine keeps its borders open under martial law: EU, US, UK, Canadian and many other passports enter visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period and others can use the official eVisa, but with civilian airspace closed, entry is only possible overland or by rail, mainly from Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania or Moldova.

travelInsurance.text: Visitors other than permanent residents of Ukraine must be able to show proof of medical insurance at the border, according to UK travel advice; e-Visa applicants upload a health insurance policy with EUR 30,000 of cover. Standard travel policies usually exclude war risks. Check the exclusions carefully or buy cover from an insurer that explicitly covers Ukraine.

onwardTicket.text: No onward ticket is formally required, but border guards may ask about the purpose of your visit, your route and where you will stay.

proofOfFunds.text: Required by law (Article 21 of the Law on the Legal Status of Foreigners). Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 884 of 2013 sets the amount at 20 times Ukraine's monthly subsistence minimum per month of stay, worked out per day as (20 × the monthly minimum ÷ 30) × (days of stay + 5). It can be shown with cash, a bank card with a statement, an accommodation booking, a tour voucher, a host's guarantee letter or a return ticket, and is checked at the border on request.

notes: Drones, night-vision devices, body armor and other dual-use equipment are tightly controlled under martial law — do not bring them without prior authorization.
Photography of military positions, checkpoints and strike damage is prohibited and can lead to detention.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are the norm in cities, and ATMs are plentiful. Keep some hryvnia in cash for small towns and for moments when strikes or power cuts knock payment terminals offline.

safety.text: Russia's full-scale invasion is ongoing. Missile and drone strikes hit cities across the whole country, and most governments advise against all travel to Ukraine. If you do go, stay away from the east and south, learn where the nearest shelter is, follow air-raid alerts and register with your embassy.

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September has the mildest weather for the long overland journeys travel now requires — though any visit should be planned around the security situation, not the season.

tips.text: Ukrainian airspace is closed to civil aviation — enter overland or by rail, most reliably on the trains from Przemyśl (Poland) to Lviv and Kyiv, or via Slovakia, Hungary, Romania or Moldova.
Install an air-raid alert app (such as Air Alert), take alerts seriously and know your nearest shelter — metro stations in Kyiv and Kharkiv double as deep shelters.
Martial law means nightly curfews (roughly midnight to 05:00, varying by region) and military checkpoints. Carry your passport at all times and never photograph checkpoints or military sites.

Ukraine treats dual nationals as Ukrainian citizens: men aged 18–60 with Ukrainian citizenship are generally barred from leaving the country under martial law. Ordinary foreign visitors are not affected by exit restrictions.
Buy medical insurance that explicitly covers Ukraine. It is an entry requirement, and standard policies usually void cover in a war zone.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Ukraine?
faq.answer: Citizens of the EU, US, UK, Canada and a broad list of other countries enter visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Many other nationalities can apply online for the official eVisa; the rest need a visa from a Ukrainian consulate. Whatever your passport, entry is currently overland only.

faq.question: How do I get to Ukraine if there are no flights?
faq.answer: Civilian airspace has been closed since February 2022, so all entry is by land or rail. The most used routes are the direct trains from Przemyśl in Poland to Lviv and Kyiv, plus road and rail crossings from Slovakia, Hungary, Romania and Moldova.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Ukraine right now?
faq.answer: No. The country is at war, missile and drone attacks reach cities far from the front line, and most governments advise against all travel. Western regions are calmer than the east and south, but nowhere is risk-free. If you must travel, prepare seriously: alerts app, shelters, insurance that covers war zones, and embassy registration.

faq.question: How does the Ukrainian eVisa work?
faq.answer: Eligible nationalities apply entirely online at evisa.mfa.gov.ua, uploading a passport scan, photo, insurance and supporting documents. The eVisa is electronic, usually issued within days, costs around US$20 for single entry and allows a stay of up to 30 days. Print the confirmation and carry it with your passport.

faq.question: Do Ukraine's martial-law exit restrictions apply to foreign visitors?
faq.answer: No. Exit restrictions apply to Ukrainian citizens — chiefly men aged 18–60 — not to foreign tourists. The important exception is dual nationals: if you also hold Ukrainian citizenship, Ukraine treats you as Ukrainian and the restrictions can apply to you.

faq.question: Should I bring cash to Ukraine?
faq.answer: Cards work well in cities and contactless payment is widespread, but carry some hryvnia — power cuts and strikes occasionally take terminals offline, and small towns still prefer cash. Declare amounts of €10,000 or more at the border.
